title: Frontend mid domain rendering pipeline
question: Walk through what happens in the browser's rendering pipeline between a CSS/JS change and pixels updating on screen, and why some changes are more expensive than others.
idealAnswer:
The pipeline generally goes style (recalculate which CSS rules apply), layout/reflow (compute geometry, position and size of every element), paint (fill in pixels), and composite (combine painted layers on the GPU)

Changing layout-affecting properties (width, position, font-size) forces layout to be recomputed, which cascades to paint and composite, this is the most expensive path

Changing paint-only properties (background-color, visibility) skips layout but still requires a repaint of the affected area

Changing composite-only properties (transform, opacity) can skip both layout and paint if the element is already promoted to its own layer, this is why animating transform/opacity is much cheaper than animating top/left or width

Reading layout properties (like offsetHeight) right after writing styles forces a synchronous layout recalculation ('layout thrashing'), doing this repeatedly in a loop is a classic performance bug

Browsers batch DOM changes and only actually run this pipeline once per frame, ideally hitting 60fps (about 16.7ms per frame) for smooth animation
